vignette:
She is seventy-seven now, a soft-spoken Middle Eastern woman who still works as a tutor, meeting children one by one at her kitchen table and helping them sound out English words or solve arithmetic problems. She is careful with them, patient in a way that feels hard won. When she talks about her life, she does not begin with the war right away. She begins with the ordinary things that existed before it: a small apartment, her parents nearby, the sound of vendors in the street, the routines that made a life feel dependable. She had once imagined she would marry, but history kept interrupting personal plans, and over time she became the daughter who stayed, the sister who was available, the woman who made herself useful.

When the fighting reaches her neighborhood, she is a young woman. At first the danger feels intermittent, something to be tracked by rumor and by the expressions on other people's faces. Then it becomes the structure of daily life. She learns to tell, from the distance and force of a blast, whether to move away from the windows or drop to the floor. She remembers the particular whistle before impact, the shaking of walls, the sudden silence after. There are days when she leaves home to buy bread and finds a building she passed yesterday split open, its rooms exposed to the street. People disappear quickly then: neighbors leave, cousins stop writing, someone is alive one week and buried the next.

One afternoon the shelling comes close enough that she and her family press themselves into a hallway, shoulders touching, waiting for the next explosion. She can still remember the dust in her mouth and her mother whispering prayers too fast to understand. Afterward they learn that people on the next block have been killed. In the months that follow, the threat never settles into the past. She sees injured civilians carried in blankets. She hears screaming from outside and does not go to the window because she already knows that looking will not help. Sleep becomes shallow and practical. She keeps her shoes beside the bed. She begins to live as if at any second she may need to run.

Even after she eventually leaves the war zone, her body does not seem to understand that she has left. In safer places, she startles at slamming doors and low-flying aircraft. Fireworks make her stomach drop before her mind can label the sound. For years she tells herself this is normal, that anyone who has lived through what she lived through would be vigilant. She builds a life around being alert. She remains single, partly from circumstance and partly because closeness comes to feel risky; she does not say this directly at first, but it emerges in fragments. She has loved people deeply and learned that the world can snatch them away without warning.

Tutoring becomes one of the few roles that gives her steady meaning. Children come to her after school, noisy and distracted, and she likes the order of books, pencils, and lesson plans. Yet even here the war enters the room. If a child drops a heavy backpack, she jerks in her chair, hand pressed to her chest, embarrassed by how quickly her body reacts. When construction starts on a nearby street, the pounding sends her mind somewhere else. She loses her place in the lesson and stares toward the window, not seeing the present neighborhood but another one, decades ago, where every loud sound asked a question about survival.

At night she rarely sleeps straight through. She wakes from dreams thick with smoke, searching for family members she cannot gather together. Sometimes she is back in the hallway; sometimes she is running through streets that rearrange themselves and never lead to safety. On those mornings she is tired in a way that feels older than age. She checks locks repeatedly before bed and keeps the television on low for company, though sudden images from the news can undo her. Reports of bombings anywhere in the world grip her with an immediate, personal dread. She knows the geography is different, the language different, but her body responds as if history is happening again in the next room.

She avoids crowded events because she cannot relax in them. She sits near exits in waiting rooms and restaurants. If she hears raised voices in public, her muscles tighten and she begins scanning faces, doors, windows. She tells herself she is being sensible. At the same time, she feels ashamed of how narrow her life has become. There are days she wants to visit friends or attend community gatherings and then spends hours arguing with herself, exhausted before she has even put on her coat.

What stands out most is how alone she has been with it. She has spent decades translating fear into discipline, grief into usefulness. She shows up for her students, makes tea, remembers homework assignments, asks about exams. From the outside she appears composed, even resilient. But in the quieter moments she describes feeling as though part of her is still frozen in that earlier life, listening for the whistle before impact, never convinced that safety can last long enough to be trusted.
